titleStmt.title: Response time and performance analysis of inter-dependent hard real-time control tasks communicating over a predictable Publish-Subscribe channel in MPSoC platforms

analytic.title: Response time and performance analysis of inter-dependent hard real-time control tasks communicating over a predictable Publish-Subscribe channel in MPSoC platforms

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper explores the challenges and methodologies for analyzing the timing and performance of safety-critical real-time robotics and control applications on Multiprocessor System-on-Chip (MPSoC) platforms, i.e., CompSOC in this study. Leveraging a predictable Publish-Subscribe communication protocol, implemented based on a wait-free FIFO channel, we focus on the Worst Case Response Time (WCRT) analysis of interdependent hard real-time tasks in a processing chain, scheduled by a Timed Division Multiplexing (TDM) scheduler. For this purpose, after we define the execution model of Publish-Subscribe based real-time applications on CompSOC, we propose two distinctive WCRT analysis approaches: a deterministic calculation approach, and a stochastic approach based on Timed Automata (TA) theory and UPPAAL Stochastic Model Checker (UPPAAL-SMC) for a tighter WCRT bound. Moreover, building upon the stochastic TA model, we propose an approach for performance analysis, particularly focusing on factors such as message loss-rate and sensor-to-actuator throughput to present the percentage of the sample data that passes all the stages in the processing chain and affect the system behaviour. Our experimental validations, conducted on an implemented instance of the CompSOC MPSoC platform on the programmable logic (FPGA) of a Pynq board, affirm the effectiveness of our approach.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the evolving landscape of embedded systems, Multiprocessor System-on-Chip (MPSoC) platforms have emerged as a cornerstone for robotic applications requiring high computational throughput within strict power and area constraints [1]. These platforms, characterized by their integration of multiple processing elements on a single chip, cater to the increasing demand for processing power in applications spanning from automotive systems to medical robotics. A critical subset of these applications entails hard real-time tasks, where the correctness of the system not only depends on the logical correctness of the computations but also on the time at which the results are produced. The deterministic execution of these tasks, often inter-dependent and communicating over various communication channels, is mandatory for ensuring the reliability and safety of the system in these applications. Moreover, performance analysis on factors such as message loss-rate and sensor-to-actuator throughput is crucial. These factors significantly impact the reliability and efficiency of safety-critical systems.

Analyzing the timing and performance of safety-critical real-time applications in MPSoC platforms is more complex than in traditional single-processor real-time systems [2]. This is due to the use of shared computation and communication resources in MPSoC platforms for efficiency purposes. While some research works [3] [4] have partially addressed this complexity through composability concepts [5], analyzing application response time remains a challenging task for preemptive and inter-dependent real-time tasks that communicate through shared resources. The introduction of the Publish-Subscribe communication model [6] in this context could further address some of these challenges by enabling a decoupled and scalable approach to managing communications among tasks, potentially simplifying the analysis and management of Worst Case Response Time (WCRT) in these complex systems.

In this paper, we first define the execution model of Pub-Sub based real-time applications on CompSOC [7] as a composabale and predictable MPSoC platform. Then, we determine the application's WCRT using both a deterministic calculation technique and a statistical model checking approach. Overall, our contributions in this paper are listed as follows:

• Deterministic WCRT analysis of inter-dependent hard realtime tasks that communicate through a Publish-Subscribe channel on a predictable MPSoC platform. This approach considers Time Devision Multiplexing (TDM) [8] as the underlying preemptive scheduler on CompSOC platform. • Stochastic WCRT analysis of inter-dependent hard realtime tasks that communicate through a Publish-Subscribe channel. To provide a tighter and less-pessimistic upperbound on the WCRT value of each task, a stochastic model is proposed based on Timed Automata theory [9], and UPPAL Stochastic Model Checker (UPPAAL-SMC) [10] is utilized to verify timing and safety properties of the system while giving practical insights on the system behavior.

• Stochastic performance analysis of the inter-dependent realtime tasks that communicate through a Pub-Sub channel on a predictable MPSoC platform. Building upon the proposed stochastic model for timing behaviour, a technique is proposed to analyze performance metrics such as sensor-toactuator throughput and message loss-rate. • Real-life experimental validation of the proposed approaches on an instance of CompSOC MPSoC platform implemented on the FPGA region of a Pynq development board. An application is composed of multiple processing chains. A processing chain, denoted as T x = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ m }, comprises m inter-dependent real-time tasks, where each task τ i may function as an absolute transmitter/publisher, an absolute receiver/subscriber, or a transceiver task. Each task τ i is represented as τ i < Γ i , [α i , ω i ], Ω i >, where Γ i denotes all tasks that transmit data to τ i via input channels, Ω i denotes all tasks that receive data from τ i through output channels, and [α i , ω i ] indicates the Best Case Execution Time (BCET) and Worst Case Execution Time (WCET) for the computational operations of task τ i respectively. The communication between inter-dependent real-time tasks in a processing chain is done through a predictable Publish-Subscribe communication protocol, implemented based on a wait-free FIFO channel [11] for MPSoC platforms. It is important to note that in hard real-time tasks, it is common practice to define a deadline parameter, which specifies the latest time by which a task must be completed. This deadline is particularly important when the goal is to conduct a schedulability analysis, ensuring that all tasks can be completed within their specified deadlines. However, since this paper focuses on analyzing the worstcase response time of tasks rather than their schedulability, the deadline is not required for the analysis presented here.

As a motivational example, in Fig. 1, an illustrative task graph from the robotics domain depicts an autonomous vehicle equipped with multiple sensors, featuring two processing chains T 1 = {τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 4 , τ 6 , τ 7 } and T 2 = {τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 , τ 5 }. The first chain, T 1 , focuses on obstacle avoidance, where data from radar and lidar sensors are fused by a sensor fusion task, τ 4 , and the fused data is then used by an obstacle detection task, τ 6 , to identify obstacles and signal the braking system to adjust the vehicle's speed or stop if necessary. The second chain, T 2 , involves all three sensors, including the IMU sriver task τ 3 , with their data processed by an odometry calculation task τ 5 to determine the vehicle's position, and the output from this task is sent to a navigation stack operating in a separate subsystem outside the MPSoC platform. In this example, for task τ 4 , Γ 4 = {τ 1 , τ 2 } and Ω 4 = {τ 6 }. The first important factor to analyze in this system, for each real-time task τ i such as Sensor Fusion, is to analyze the maximum response time that it takes to receive the data from the input channels, conduct a processing on the data, and publish the output to the output channels. Moreover, for a processing chain such as T 1 , it is important to analyze the percentage of the sample data generated by the Lidar Driver, τ 1 , that manages to pass through all the tasks in the processing chain and affect the system behaviour by the Break System in τ 7 . This factor is called sensor-to-actuator throughput, and depends on the lossrate on the Pub-Sub channels between the tasks.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: As discussed in Sec. I, we utilize CompSOC [7] as the underlying MPSoC platform. CompSOC is a composable and predictable MPSoC architecture that guarantees predictability in the clock cycle level of the processor. Each CompSOC tile is equipped with a 32-bit RISC-V [12] processor, operating at a frequency of 40 MHz. Alongside the processor, there is 128KB of combined instruction and data memory available per tile. Atop each RISC-V processor, a Virtualization Kernel (VKERNEL) [5] is implemented to virtualize the tile resources into v isolated Virtual Execution Platforms (VEP), with v = 4 for this study. These VEPs operate on each RISC-V processor through a preemptive and static Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) scheduler that enables the concurrent execution of multiple VEPs on the same processor. A VEP represents a dedicated and fully isolated segment of the tile's resources, both processor and memory, assigned to run a particular real-time task. The communication between the tiles happens through a time predictable memory ring connected to a shared memory with 16KB capacity.

As shown in Fig. 2, for any given processor p, the first TDM slot (slot p,0 ) is reserved for the system application running in SysVEP, and each VEP for processor p, labelled as V EP p,k , occupies the slot slot p,k with length sl p,k clock cycles. The duration allocated to the system application slot denoted by sl p,0 and the context switch time between different TDM slots denoted by cst are specified as 5000 and 2000 clock cycles, respectively. Therefore, for any given processor p, the TDM period is represented by π p = ∑ 3 i=0 sl p,i + 4 × cst. For the static scheduling of all tasks within a processing chain, we create a static mapping defined as schedule = τ i → V EP p,k implying that task τ i is assigned to V EP p,k running in slot p,k .

div.head: IV. PROBLEM STATEMENT
div.p: Given the application model, presented in Sec. II, and the system model, presented in Sec. III, the first focus of this paper lies in determining an upper-bound for the Worst Case Response Time (WCRT) of every task τ i of a processing chain that runs in V EP p,k . This encompasses calculating the WCRT for receiving data from all input channels (input communication delay), the WCRT for executing the computational operations on the received data (computation delay), and the WCRT for publishing the results to the output channels (output communication delay). In general, the calculation of the WCRT for each task follows a standardized two-step procedure [13]. Initially, the WCET of the task is determined Fig. 2: Pub-Sub tasks scheduled by TDM on CompSOC tiles utilizing execution path exploration methods [14], then, the analysis of the task's WCRT takes into account the underlying resource scheduling policy and the task's release pattern. In this paper, we introduce two different methods for analyzing the WCRT value of each task τ i . The first method is a guaranteed deterministic calculation technique, and the second approach is a stochastic approach utilizing Timed Automata theory [9] leading to a tighter upper-bound for the WCRT.

In traditional real-time systems with a chain of interdependent real-time tasks, the end-to-end response time is crucial for ensuring the processing chain meets the deadline. It refers to the total duration from request initiation to completion across inter-dependent tasks. This includes processing time, scheduling delays, and communication overhead. However, in the realm of real-time robotics and control, where tasks communicate via a publish-subscribe channel, the concept of end-to-end response time loses relevance. This is because data points on a given pub-sub channel may get overwritten due to inconsistency in processing speed between publishers and subscribers. Therefore, in real-time robotics and control, the emphasis shifts from end-to-end response time to factors like sensor-to-actuator throughput. This metric, defined as the second focus of this paper, signifies a lower-bound on the number of sensor data samples that successfully traverse the processing chain, impacting the system actuation behaviour within a given time frame. It is clear that finding the minimum sensor-toactuation throughput hinges on establishing an upper-bound for the WCRT of every inter-dependent real-time task within the processing chain addressed by the first focus of this paper.

div.head: V. WCET FOR INTER-DEPENDENT TASKS ON COMPSOC
div.p: As explained in Sec. IV, the calculation of the WCRT for each task follows a two-step process, where initially the WCET of the task is determined using execution path exploration methods, assuming that the whole processor is assigned to the task without any scheduling preemption. Overall, as presented in Eq. 1, the WCET of a real-time task τ i is the combination of the WCET for the computational behaviour of τ i , along with the WCET for the underlying wait-free FIFO channel used as the Publish-Subscribe input/output channel between the tasks.

div.head: VII. STOCHASTIC ANALYSIS OF WCRT
div.p: In this section, we introduce a stochastic method to provide a tighter upper-bound for the WCRT of inter-dependent realtime tasks in a processing chain utilizing Timed Automata (TA) theory [9] and the UPPAAL Stochastic Model Checker (UPPAAL-SMC) [10] features. For this purpose, we need to precisely model the system behaviour, including the TDM scheduler and each real-time task τ i , using TA theory. Timed Automata Theory [9] extends classical automata theory by incorporating the concept of time into the operational semantics of automata. A Timed Automaton is composed of states and transitions, similar to a traditional automaton, but it also includes clocks, which are real-valued variables that increase linearly with time. Transitions between states can be conditioned on these clock values, and the clocks can be reset. This mechanism allows for the specification of timing constraints, such as timeouts and deadlines, within the system being modeled. Additionally, an invariant can be associated with each state to facilitate the evaluation of progress properties. This means that through an invariant, it is possible to define the upper and lower time limits for how long the system can remain in a given state. TA model for computation WCRT: In this section, we present a TA model representing the computational behavior of a real-time task τ i executed within V EP p,k and scheduled in slot p,k . It is crucial to highlight that the TA model introduced here serves as a foundational model, later utilized to depict the WCRT value of any isolated code segment on the underlying MPSoC platform. Illustrated in Fig. 4, the model in State 1 outlines four potential scenarios, each depicting the computational behavior of task τ i in every clock cycle of the processor, depending on whether it has been allocated the processor and whether the task has completed. 1) Processor assigned, execution not finished: At the end of each clock cycle in the system, if the remained execution time of task τ i , indicated by t remained[i], is more than one clock cycle, and the processor is assigned to the host slot of τ i , the task executes one more clock cycle by decrementing t remained[i] and the model stays in the same state. This scenario is captured using the guard G1, action A1, and synchronization signal S1, as depicted in As shown in the task TA model in Fig. 4, the initial state of the model is State 0 where the model needs to receive the release signal from the scheduler to release its first iteration after the scheduler finished the context switch time and assign the processor p to the host TDM slot k for τ i . In the next sections, we will use the template part of the this model, to create the complex hard real-time tasks with Pub-Sub communication in a modular way. As clarified in the model, the red states are responsible to report the WCRT of the current iteration, and prepare the model for releasing the new iteration.

TA model for Pub-Sub communication: In Sec. II, we discussed how the WCRT of inter-dependent real-time tasks relies on both computation and communication delays. In the previous section, we introduced a TA model that can be flexibly employed to examine the response time characteristics of any distinct code segment with [α i , ω i ]. Consequently, we can expand this TA model to assess the response times of each individual code segment within the Publisher and Subscriber algorithms outlined in Alg. 1 and 2, respectively, to find the WCRT of both computation and communication behaviour of inter-dependent tasks. For this purpose, initially, we need to construct an execution model for each algorithm, Publisher and Subscriber, utilizing the TA theory, disregarding the underlying resource scheduler. Such a TA execution model for the publisher and subscriber are presented in [11]. Then, we substitute each state of the TA execution model with the presented template illustrated in Fig. 4 to take into account the resource scheduler affect. By employing this approach, the TA models for analyzing the response times of a publisher task, real-time task with publishing data to a Pub-Sub channel, and subscriber task, real-time task that subscribes and process data from a Pub-Sub channel, are depicted in Fig. 5. It's crucial to note that the TA model depicted in Fig. 5 represents both the computation and the communication behavior of a single publish/output channel and a single subscribe/input channel. Expanding the model to more than one input/output channel is done using a similar approach in a modular way.

Property verification and stochastic WCRT analysis: When we have the TA model of the system, including the scheduler model in Fig. 3, and TA model for all involved real-time tasks, presented in Fig. 5, we can leverage the verification capabilities of the UPPAAL model checker engine to specify and validate certain safety properties, such as the absence of deadlocks and starvation freedom, using temporal logic formulas. For WCRT analysis, due to the potential exponential growth of the state space size, exhaustive exploration becomes impractical. Hence, we opt to utilize UPPAAL-SMC features to probabilistically determine WCRT values. Instead of obtaining an exact WCRT from fully exploring the state space, UPPAAL-SMC randomly samples multiple, but configurable, subsets to decrease the state space size and provide a WCRT value with a probabilistic confidence level for each real-time task. For this purpose, we define the following property, based on the UPPAAL-SMC defined format, in Eq. 13 to find the WCRT value, that includes both computation and communication delays, of τ i in a stochastic way. In this property, we command the UPPAAL-SMC model checker engine to randomly explore the state space of the system for 1 billion clock cycles and report the maximum encountered value of wcrt[i] as the WCRT value of τ i . To make the result more reliable, we ask the model checker engine to perform the exploration 10 times.

div.head: VIII. SENSOR-TO-ACTUATOR THROUGHPUT ANALYSIS
div.p: As previously mentioned, we can utilize the proposed Timed Automata model depicted in Fig. 5 for performance assessment. For instance, by introducing two integer variables, published[c] and lost[c] initialized by zero, into the message publisher task model, we can assess the message loss or overwrite-rate of a designated Pub-Sub channel c. This modification involves incrementing the published[c] variable each time a new data is written into the channel in state PState 6, and incrementing the lost[c] variable each time a data token is overwritten in state PState 5. Through this adaptation, we assess the maximum message loss-rate over channel c using the property defined in Eq. 14 in a stochastic manner. It is worth mentioning that 1overwrite rate[c] yields the throughput over that specific channel c.

When considering the message throughput across each Pub-Sub channel within a processing chain, we can derive the sensor-to-actuator throughput by multiplying the throughput of consecutive Pub-Sub channels in the chain. This metric quantifies the proportion of sample data points generated by sensors that manage to go through all stages of the processing chain and affect the final behaviour of the system through the actuator. For instance, if sensor data is generated at a rate of 1 millisecond and the sensor-to-actuator throughput is 25%, it implies that within the configured setup, only 1 out of every 4 generated sensor data points affects the final behavior of the actuator. This suggests that the actuator behavior is influenced by sensor data approximately every 4 milliseconds.

div.head: IX. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we assess the effectiveness of our proposed approaches through practical validation using real-time tasks and processing chains implemented on a specific instance of the CompSOC MPSoC platform.

div.head: A. System Setup
div.p: There are multiple implementations of CompSOC available, including versions designed for FPGA and ASIC platforms. In our setup, we utilize the Verintec implementation [15] specifically tailored for the FPGA side of a Xilinx PYNQ-Z2 board. This configuration implements a three tile CompSOC instance. By default, this setup supports up to three isolated VEPs per processor, enabling a total of nine real-time tasks to run concurrently. However, it's possible to adjust the TDM table of the scheduler to create additional TDM slots, thus accommodating more real-time tasks. As outlined in Sec. III, the duration of TDM period is v π p = 43, 000 clock cycles, with sl p,0 = 5, 000 cycles allocated to the system application on each tile, sl p,k = 10, 000 cycles assigned to each user VEP, and a context switch between TDM slots consuming cst = 2, 000 clock cycles.

div.head: B. Execution Time Measurements
div.p: As explained in Sec. III, each tile within the CompSOC platform includes a TDM scheduler responsible for determining the allocation of resources to isolated VEPs based on a userdefined TDM table. The architectural design of CompSOC is founded on the principles of composability and predictability, ensuring that the execution time of any instruction can be accurately predicted and reproduced in terms of the required number of clock cycles. Determining the execution time for executing a segment of code on CompSOC is facilitated by the platform's utilization of a local VEP timer, which functions exclusively when the processor is allocated to the VEP. Consequently, calculating the time difference between the initial and final lines of code provides a precise and reliable measure of the execution time for running that segment on the platform. By executing the publisher and subscriber algorithms on the experimental setup, we measured various execution time parameters such as e px , representing the time required to execute line x of the publisher, and e cx , denoting the time needed to execute line x of the subscriber algorithms, as detailed in Table I. Regarding the application setup, we designed a simple processing chain with one publisher and one subscriber executed on two different CompSOC tiles that communicate over a single Pub-Sub channel. For the computational aspect of the real-time tasks in this processing chain, τ 1 = publisher and τ 2 = subscriber, we assign a random execution times falling within a specified range [α i , ω i ] for each task τ i in the processing chain. For example, to force the system to exhibit its worst-case behavior, which occurs when the channel becomes full due to the publisher generating data faster than the subscriber can process, we allocated a computational workload to the publisher task that exceeds that of the subscriber task, as illustrated in Table I.

div.head: C. Worst Case Response Time Validation
div.p: To verify the effectiveness of our proposed approaches for WCRT analysis, both the deterministic calculation and stochastic analysis methods were employed. We conducted experiments with publisher and subscriber tasks communicating over a Pub-Sub channel with a buffer size of 5, executed on two isolated VEPs across two parallel CompSOC tiles. As presented in Table II, for each real-time task, we initially calculated the upper-bound WCRT value using the method described in Sec. VI, which provides a strict and guaranteed upper-limit on the task's WCRT value. In the stochastic approach, the UPPAAL-SMC engine provides a range of WCRT values along with an associated probability or confidence level, rather than a single WCRT value. For instance, as depicted in Fig. 6, the stochastic WCRT value for the publisher task, based on the parameters listed in Table I, fell within the range [81450, 83416] clock cycles. Each value in this range is accompanied by its upper and lower limits, as well as the cumulative confidence level, as illustrated in Fig. 6. For validation purposes, we utilize the maximum value within the range, such as 83416 in this instance. Subsequently, the platform was executed to publish over one million messages for 10 iterations, with the response time of each iteration measured for comparison. Fig. 7 demonstrates that the actual measured response time of the publisher task, measured by the global timer of CompSOC, consistently falls within the bounds reported by both of our approaches. Notably, the stochastic approach offers a more realistic WCRT value compared to the calculated upper-bound value. The experiment was repeated on the subscriber side of the Pub-Sub channel, and the results, depicted in Fig. 8 and9, validate the effictiveness of both proposed approaches. Notably, the stochastic approach offers a more realistic bound.

div.head: D. Message Loss-rate Validation
div.p: To assess the effectiveness of our approach in performance analysis, we implemented the necessary modifications discussed in Sec. VIII on the presented TA models in Fig. 5 to examine the message loss-rate across a specific Pub-Sub channel using the execution parameters outlined in Table I. As illustrated in Fig. 5, the generated output by UPPAAL-SMC, based on the defined property in Eq. 14, is presented as cumulative probability confidence intervals for the maximum message loss-rate. In this instance, with a confidence level of [0.21, 0.83], the maximum analyzed overwrite-rate on the channel is %75, which aligns with our real-life experiments on CompSOC, where the maximum overwrite rate observed was %73 over one million published messages across 10 iterations. Furthermore, to assess how the subscriber workload impacts the message loss-rate and to assess the robustness of our proposed approach, we gradually reduced the workload of the subscriber. We then compared the analyzed maximum overwrite-rate with the corresponding values obtained from real-life experiments on CompSOC. As depicted in Table III, reducing the subscriber workload correlates directly with a decrease in the overwrite-rate, and our approach demonstrates robustness in handling parameter variations.

div.head: E. Sensor-to-Actuator Throughput Validation
div.p: As outlined in Sec. VIII, once we have the overwrite-rate for each channel, we can assess the sensor-to-actuator throughput of a processing chain by multiplying the throughput of consecutive channels. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our model, we constructed two processing chains consisting of 3 and 6 real-time tasks running on different VEPs as presented in Fig. 11. Employing our proposed stochastic approach from Sec. VII, we analyzed the message loss-rate over each Pub-Sub channel and calculated the sensor-to-actuator throughput for each processor chain using the method discussed in Sec. VIII. Subsequently, we compared the calculated expected values with the corresponding real-life experimental values obtained on CompSOC. As depicted in Fig. 11, our proposed approach reliably provides a lower-bound for the sensor-to-actuator throughput of real-time processing chains.

div.head: F. Scalability of the stochastic analysis approach
div.p: The initial experiment with a single publisher and a single subscriber task running on two different tiles required less than 5 minutes using UPPAAL-SMC. When the number of tasks was increased to 9, distributed across all virtual execution platforms, the analysis time in UPPAAL-SMC rose to approximately 10 minutes. In the context of robotics, where task graphs are typically not excessively large, this analysis time is considered reasonable. It allows for the provision of a tighter upper-bound on the WCRT and other performance metrics, ensuring that the system can meet stringent timing requirements while maintaining efficient performance.

div.head: X. RELATED WORK
div.p: The works related to the scope of this paper are classified into the following two categories:

Pub-Sub communication for real-time MPSoCs: Perez et al. [16] introduced a system design incorporating the Data Distribution Service (DDS) [17] standard into the XtratuM hypervisor, aiming for seamless communication within partitioned real-time systems. Nonetheless, their proposal overlooks timing prerequisites, such as guaranteed WCRT, and resource constraints. embeddedRTPS [18] offers a compact DDS implementation, targeting small embedded devices as primary DDS participants. This implementation relies on FreeRTOS [19] and lightweightIP on a single STM32 micro-controller. However, it lacks an analytical framework. Hamerski et al. [20] proposed a Pub-Sub communication strategy to decouple application development temporally and spatially for MPSoC platforms. Dehnavi et al. [11] introduced a wait-free FIFO method for facilitating communication between a single publisher and a single subscriber across cores using shared memory, laying the groundwork for real-time Pub-Sub communication on MPSoC platforms. Through an examination of the execution paths for each process, it demonstrated that the time taken for each read or write operation is limited by a specific WCET value. In this paper, we utilize their approach as the Pub-Sub communication mechanism between our real-time tasks.

Response time analysis of Pub-Sub based interdependent hard real-time task graphs on MPSoC: Oh et al. [21] introduced a cost model for Pub-Sub systems in real-time contexts, demonstrating empirical validation on mobile embedded devices. Their approach did not address the adaptation of Publish-Subscribe communication for hard realtime tasks on MPSoC platforms, and it lacked a solution for conducting WCRT analysis, a crucial requirement for safetycritical applications. Casini et al. [22] introduced a method for response time analysis of ROS2 [23] processing chains employing reservation-based scheduling. Nonetheless, their assumption of an ideal DDS network with assured delays between ROS2 nodes in distributed systems overlooks the resource-intensive and unpredictable nature of DDS [17], making it unsuitable for adapting to safety-critical hard realtime tasks on resource-constraint MPSoCs. Hamerski et al. [24] directed their attention towards integrating the Publish-Subscribe communication paradigm into MPSoC platforms, but their method primarily revolved around experimentally evaluating serialization libraries as a crucial aspect of pub-sub communication mechanisms on MPSoC. Furthermore, several studies [25]- [28] have investigated the end-to-end latency between ROS2 nodes and DDS entities. Nevertheless, the inherently resource-intensive and unpredictable nature of DDS This paper tackles the analysis of Worst Case Response Time (WCRT) for inter-dependent real-time tasks communicating via a predictable Publish-Subscribe communication channel on resource-constrained MPSoC platforms. We introduced two methodologies for this purpose: a deterministic calculation technique and a tighter stochastic approach based on Timed Automata (TA) theory. Additionally, based on the stochastic TA model, we presented a solution for performance analysis, particularly focusing on factors like sensorto-actuator throughput. Our real-life experiments conducted on the CompSOC MPSoC verified the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating its robustness in accommodating changes in parameters and system size.

III, we discussed the allocation of real-time tasks to VEPs for scheduling on processing tiles via a TDM scheduler. To accurately represent this process, we utilize TA theory to construct a model of the underlying TDM scheduler on tile p, as illustrated in Fig. 3. This model comprises two distinct states: State 0, signifying instances where the processor is allocated to a VEP for executing the hosted real-time task, and State 1, indicating the scheduler's state during a context switch between two TDM slots. Within this model, variables such as current slot [p] denote the TDM slot to which the processor is assigned in the current clock cycle, sl [p] [k] represents the length of TDM slot k on tile p in clock cycles, and in switch slot [p] indicates whether the scheduler is in a context switch period. In this case, if the scheduler is not still in the context switch slot, indicated by in switch slot[p], it means that the processor is still assigned to the host slot of τ i , and the task can immediately release its new iteration. Therefore, the model moves to the intermediate state State 2, which is an Uppaal special type Urgent State with zero delay, by decrementing t remained[i] and storing the value of the clock variable t wcrt[i] as the WCRT of task τ i . When the model enter State 2, since the processor is still assigned to the host slot of τ i , it immediately releases the new iteration of the task by setting t remained[i] to a random value between bcet[i] and wcet[i]. It is clear that bcet[i] and wcet[i], refer to α i and ω i , respectively. It is worth mentioning that t wcrt[i] is a clock variable defined to keep track of the passed response time since the release point of τ i 's current iteration 3) Processor assigned, execution finished, end of slot: Similar to the previous scenario, the task execution is finished and it needs to release its new iteration, but the execution of the final clock cycle of the task happens at the last clock cycle of the host TMD slot k. In this case, after storing the WCRT of the current iteration in State 3, the model needs to wait in State 4 before the processor is assigned to slot p,k in the next TDM period and the release signal is received from the scheduler model. Then the new iteration of τ i is released, and the model moves to State 0. 4) Processor unassigned: In this case, since signal S1 is not received, the model stays in the same state State 1 without performing any action.
